newsitem.title: USA: Intel, AMD settle MMX litigation.
newsitem.headline: Intel, AMD settle MMX litigation.

text.p: Intel Corp and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. said they had agreed to settle litigation over the use of the term MMX to describe computer chips compatible with Intel's MMX semiconductor technology.

Under the terms of the settlement, AMD will acknowledge MMX as a trademark owned by Intel, but will have rights to use the mark in the worldwide marketing of its sixth-generation K6 processors, the companies said in a joint statement.
For example, the companies said AMD and its customers in any country can promote its K6 processor as "MMX(TM) Enabled" or "MMX(TM) Enhanced."

The swift settlement of litigation brought by Intel in mid-March comes at a key time for both companies. AMD has just launched its K-6 chip, which it claims is in the same league as Intel's Pentium chips but promises to keep them at least 25 percent cheaper than equivalent Intel chips.
Likewise, Intel is launching a new line of computer microprocessor chips, the Pentium II, next month.
The deal follows a similar settlement earlier this month between Intel and Richardson, Texas-based Cyrix Corp, which also will be able to use MMX to promote its chips.
"We are very pleased to have this issue resolved for both ourselves and our customers," Thomas McCoy, AMD vice president and general counsel, said in a statement.

"Our agreement with Intel secures for AMD and its customers the ability, on a worldwide basis and in all channels of distribution, to continue promoting the MMX capabilities of the AMD-K6 processor, including the use of the term in the AMD-K6 processor logo," McCoy said.
He also said the settlement avoids any confusion in the marketplace that might have occurred had the litigation resulted in a protracted legal battle.
Spokesmen for the two companies said the deal settles other unrelated trademark issues, including any use of Intel's Pentium trademark to describe its family of microprocessors.

No money changed hands in the deal, which followed months of negotiation, the spokesmen said. For Intel's Advanced Graphics Port, which will be an increasingly important feature, it chose not to seek a protected trademark, they added.
"The important thing for us all along has been the acknowledgement of our ownership of that trademark, MMX," said Intel spokesman Chuck Malloy.

The two companies had already agreed, as part of a broad cross licensing pact in early 1996, that AMD would have rights to the underlying lines of code related to the MMX technology, which contains various new multimedia capabilities.

On April 1 a federal judge in Delaware declined Intel's request for a restraining order, which would have blocked AMD from promoting its AMD K6 chip during its launch as an MMX processor. Under the deal, AMD acknowledges Intel's mark.
AMD spokesman Scott Allen said the company plans to ship hundreds of thousands of chips by the end of this quarter and millions of its K6 chips during the second half of 1997.
"We are going to price our K6 at least 25 percent less than the equivalent Intel product," he added.
